section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: South Dakota is one of only a few states where a teenager can apply for a learner's permit at age 14. What type of permit is issued at age 14 in South Dakota?
options: a:A full learner's permit with no restrictions,b:A restricted minor's permit for driving to school only,c:A minor's permit allowing supervised driving practice,d:No permit is available at 14 — minimum age is 15
note: South Dakota allows teenagers to apply for a minor's permit at age 14, making it one of the youngest permit ages in the US. At 14, the permit holder may only drive with a licensed adult who is at least 18 years old in the front seat. This reflects South Dakota's rural character where teens often need to drive to assist with farm and family duties.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: What is the legal BAC limit for drivers age 21 and older in South Dakota?
note: South Dakota sets the per se DUI limit at 0.08% BAC for drivers 21 and older. Commercial vehicle operators face a stricter 0.04% limit. A BAC of 0.08% alone is sufficient grounds for a DUI charge regardless of apparent impairment.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: You are driving on a rural South Dakota road during harvest season and encounter slow-moving farm equipment. What is the legal maximum speed for farm equipment on South Dakota roads?
options: a:15 mph,b:25 mph,c:35 mph,d:45 mph
note: Farm equipment is common on South Dakota rural roads, especially during planting and harvest seasons. Such equipment is typically limited to 25 mph or less. When approaching slow-moving vehicles displaying an orange triangle (slow-moving vehicle emblem), reduce speed early and pass only when it is safe to do so with adequate sight distance.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: What does an orange triangular emblem on the back of a slow-moving vehicle mean?
options: a:The vehicle is a school bus — stop when lights flash,b:The vehicle travels at 25 mph or less — approach with caution,c:The vehicle is authorized to drive on the highway shoulder only,d:Hazardous materials are being transported
note: The orange/red slow-moving vehicle (SMV) triangle emblem indicates the vehicle travels at 25 mph or less. This is especially important on South Dakota rural roads where farm tractors, combines, and other agricultural equipment commonly share the road with passenger vehicles. Approach these vehicles with reduced speed and patience.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: South Dakota's zero tolerance law for drivers under 21 sets the illegal BAC at:
options: a:0.00% — any measurable amount,b:0.02%,c:0.04%,d:0.05%
note: South Dakota's zero tolerance law sets a BAC threshold of 0.02% for drivers under 21. Any BAC at or above 0.02% results in DUI charges for underage drivers. This is designed to deter any drinking before driving by persons under the legal drinking age.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: What is the maximum speed limit on South Dakota rural interstate highways?
options: a:65 mph,b:70 mph,c:75 mph,d:80 mph
note: South Dakota allows a maximum speed of 75 mph on rural interstate highways for passenger vehicles. Trucks are subject to lower limits. South Dakota's wide-open spaces and straight highways make it one of the states with higher speed limits, but drivers must still adjust speed for conditions including weather, traffic, and road surface.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Under South Dakota's GDL program, a minor's permit holder (age 14–15) must have a licensed adult present while driving. This adult must be:
options: a:Any person age 18 or older with a valid license,b:A parent or legal guardian only,c:A licensed driving instructor only,d:A licensed driver age 18 or older seated in the front passenger area
note: When a minor's permit holder (age 14–15) is driving, a licensed driver who is at least 18 years old must be seated in the front seat alongside them. This supervisor must hold a valid driver's license. After turning 16 and passing the driving skills test, the minor can advance to a restricted minor's license.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: You are driving on a South Dakota gravel road — common across the state — and your vehicle begins to skid on loose gravel. What is the correct response?
options: a:Brake hard immediately to stop the skid,b:Accelerate to regain traction,c:Ease off the accelerator gently and steer in the direction you want to go,d:Turn the steering wheel sharply in the opposite direction of the skid
note: On loose gravel — extremely common on South Dakota rural roads — skid recovery requires gently easing off the accelerator and steering smoothly in the direction you want to travel. Sudden braking or sharp steering inputs worsen skids on loose surfaces. Slow down before gravel sections, not during them.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: South Dakota has vast open range areas where livestock may be on or near the road. When you see a 'Open Range' or livestock warning sign, you should:
options: a:Continue at normal speed — livestock are not your legal concern,b:Reduce speed and be prepared to stop for animals on the roadway,c:Sound your horn to scare animals away from the road,d:Stop completely and wait for animals to clear on their own
note: South Dakota's open range laws allow livestock to roam freely, meaning animals may be on or near the road at any time. When you see open range or livestock warning signs, reduce your speed and be prepared to stop. In South Dakota, the driver (not the rancher) is responsible for avoiding collisions with livestock on open range land.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: What is the default speed limit on South Dakota residential streets when no speed limit sign is posted?
options: a:15 mph,b:25 mph,c:30 mph,d:35 mph
note: South Dakota's default speed limit in urban and residential areas is 25 mph when no other speed limit is posted. Always check posted signs — school zones and areas near parks typically have lower limits. In rural areas without posted signs, the default is 55 mph.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When approaching a school bus with flashing red lights and a stop arm extended on a South Dakota road, traffic in both directions must stop at least:
options: a:10 feet from the bus,b:20 feet from the bus,c:30 feet from the bus,d:50 feet from the bus
note: South Dakota law requires vehicles traveling in both directions on an undivided road to stop at least 20 feet from a school bus with activated red lights. Do not proceed until the lights stop flashing and the arm retracts. On a divided highway with a median, only traffic behind the bus must stop.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: You are approaching a railroad crossing with flashing lights and a lowered gate. What must you do?
options: a:Slow to 15 mph and look carefully before crossing,b:Stop at least 15 feet before the gate and wait until the train has completely passed and gates have fully risen,c:Wait for the flashing lights to stop, then proceed even if the gate is still partially down,d:Proceed if you can see the train is more than a quarter mile away
note: When a railroad crossing has activated flashing lights and/or a lowered gate, you must stop at least 15 feet from the nearest rail and wait until the train has completely passed and the gate has fully risen before crossing. Never try to race a train or cross while the gate is descending or rising.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: South Dakota's Move Over law requires drivers approaching a stopped emergency or law enforcement vehicle with flashing lights to:
options: a:Slow to 15 mph regardless of the posted speed limit,b:Move to the farthest available lane from the stopped vehicle, or slow significantly if lane change is not safe,c:Stop completely until the emergency vehicle leaves,d:Only yield if the vehicle is on the right side of the road
note: South Dakota's Move Over law requires drivers to move to the farthest available lane away from a stopped emergency, law enforcement, or maintenance vehicle with flashing lights. If a lane change is not safely possible, reduce speed significantly. Violating the Move Over law carries steep fines in South Dakota.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: A flashing red traffic light means:
options: a:Slow down and proceed with caution,b:Yield to cross traffic but a full stop is not required,c:Stop, yield to all traffic and pedestrians, then proceed when safe,d:The signal is malfunctioning — treat as a four-way stop with all-way yield
note: A flashing red light is treated exactly like a stop sign in South Dakota. Come to a complete stop, yield to all cross traffic and pedestrians, and proceed only when the intersection is clear. A flashing yellow requires caution and reduced speed, but not a full stop.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: In South Dakota, when is it legal to pass on the right?
options: a:Never — passing on the right is always prohibited,b:When the vehicle ahead is making or waiting to make a left turn,c:Whenever the lane to the right is clear,d:Passing on the right is always legal on two-lane roads
note: Passing on the right is permitted in South Dakota only when the vehicle being passed is making or about to make a left turn, and there is enough paved road to the right to safely pass without leaving the roadway. Passing on a shoulder or unpaved surface is prohibited.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: What is the recommended following distance under normal driving conditions in South Dakota?
options: a:1 second,b:2 seconds,c:3 seconds,d:5 seconds
note: South Dakota recommends a minimum 3-second following distance under normal conditions. On rural highways at higher speeds — common in South Dakota — the 3-second rule should be extended, as reaction distances are greater at 75 mph than at 55 mph. In adverse weather, double your following distance.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: What should you do when you are driving in blizzard conditions — frequent in South Dakota winters — and visibility drops to near zero?
options: a:Use high beams for maximum visibility and continue at reduced speed,b:Pull off the road completely, stay in your vehicle, and call for help if needed,c:Slow to 15 mph and activate hazard flashers,d:Follow closely behind a large truck to use it as a windshield
note: In near-zero-visibility blizzard conditions on South Dakota roads, the safest action is to pull completely off the road (into a rest area, parking lot, or a safe shoulder position), stay in your vehicle with hazard lights on, and wait for conditions to improve. South Dakota's plains are prone to sudden ground blizzards — never attempt to continue driving when you cannot see the road.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: South Dakota requires headlights to be on:
options: a:Only from midnight to 5 AM,b:From sunset to sunrise and any time visibility is less than 1,000 feet,c:Only during officially declared weather emergencies,d:Whenever driving on rural roads, regardless of time
note: South Dakota requires headlights from sunset to sunrise and whenever weather or other conditions reduce visibility to less than 1,000 feet. This includes fog, rain, snow, and dust — all conditions that can occur suddenly on the South Dakota plains. If conditions require wipers, headlights should also be used.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: In South Dakota, what is the maximum speed limit on most two-lane rural highways?
options: a:55 mph,b:60 mph,c:65 mph,d:70 mph
note: South Dakota's maximum speed limit on most rural two-lane highways is 65 mph. On rural interstates, the limit is 75 mph. Always check posted signs — some sections near towns, curves, or construction zones may have lower limits.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: You are turning left from a two-way street onto another two-way street in South Dakota. Where should your vehicle end up after completing the turn?
options: a:In the far right lane of the new street,b:In the nearest lane on the right side of the center line,c:In any available lane of the new street,d:In the left lane of the new street
note: When turning left, you should always turn into the nearest lane on the right side of the center line — i.e., the closest lane going in the new direction. Do not swing wide into another lane. Complete the turn by entering the nearmost lane, then signal and change lanes if needed.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When parking on a hill facing downhill with a curb in South Dakota, you should turn your front wheels:
options: a:Away from the curb (left),b:Toward the curb (right),c:Straight — parallel to the curb,d:Toward the center of the road
note: When parking downhill with a curb, turn your front wheels toward the curb (right). If your brakes fail, the vehicle will roll forward and the tire will contact the curb, preventing the car from rolling into traffic. Remember: downhill = toward the curb; uphill = away from the curb (or toward the shoulder if no curb).

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: What does a solid white line between lanes on a highway indicate?
options: a:Passing is prohibited — lane changes are not permitted,b:Discourage lane changes but do not prohibit them in most situations,c:The start of a carpool or HOV lane,d:A bicycle lane boundary
note: A solid white line between lanes discourages lane changes but generally does not prohibit them in the way a solid yellow center line prohibits passing. You may cross a solid white lane line when necessary, but do so with caution. Solid white lines near intersections or at on-ramps are stricter lane boundaries.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Implied consent laws in South Dakota mean that any driver suspected of DUI who refuses a chemical test will:
options: a:Face no consequences — refusal is a protected right,b:Automatically lose their license for a period and face additional penalties,c:Only be fined but not lose their license,d:Only face penalties if later convicted of DUI
note: South Dakota's implied consent law means that by driving on state roads, you have consented to chemical testing if suspected of DUI. Refusing results in automatic license revocation — 1 year for a first offense — and the refusal can be presented as evidence in court. Refusal rarely helps a driver and often makes the situation worse.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: South Dakota has many gravel and unpaved county roads. When transitioning from a paved road to gravel, you should:
options: a:Maintain your speed to keep momentum,b:Accelerate slightly to improve traction,c:Reduce speed before the transition and increase following distance,d:Only reduce speed if the speed limit sign changes
note: Gravel roads have significantly less traction than paved roads, especially when wet or loose. Reduce your speed before transitioning to gravel, and increase your following distance. Stopping distances on gravel are much longer than on pavement, and steering control is reduced at higher speeds on loose surfaces.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: You are driving at night on a South Dakota rural highway and see an animal's eyes reflecting in your headlights ahead. What is the best response?
options: a:Flash your high beams rapidly to scare the animal away,b:Brake hard and lean on the horn,c:Reduce speed, cover the brake, and be prepared to stop — do not swerve sharply,d:Swerve around the animal at full speed to avoid it
note: South Dakota's rural roads have significant wildlife — deer, pronghorn, and even livestock. When you see eyes reflecting in your headlights, reduce speed immediately and cover the brake (rest your foot over the brake pedal without pressing). Avoid sharp swerving, which can cause you to lose control or roll over. Slow, controlled braking is safer than a sudden swerve.

question: Where are high beam headlights appropriate to use?
options: a:Both of the above.,b:Whenever there may be pedestrians anywhere around.,c:On unfamiliar roads or where there are no oncoming vehicles
note: High beams are used on dark, open roads when there are no oncoming vehicles or vehicles directly ahead of you, such as on unfamiliar rural roads. They help you see farther ahead, but you must switch to low beams when you see oncoming traffic or when you are following another vehicle closely so you do not blind other drivers.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Drivers making left turns must yield to:
options: a:No one in particular.,b:Passing cars only.,c:Oncoming vehicles traveling straight or turning right.
note: When turning left, you must yield to oncoming traffic that is close enough to be a hazard, including vehicles going straight and those turning right, as well as bicycles and motorcycles. You may only complete your left turn when it is safe and will not force oncoming traffic to slow or stop suddenly.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: If you drive faster than surrounding traffic and keep passing on a two-lane road, what is the likely result?
options: a:Reduce fuel consumption for all drivers.,b:Help prevent traffic congestion.,c:Increase your chances of a collision.,d:Get you to your destination much more quickly and safely.
note: Driving faster than surrounding traffic and repeatedly passing on a two-lane road greatly increases your risk of a head-on or side collision. Each pass requires you to move into the oncoming lane, where your time and space to react are limited. Staying with the flow of traffic at a safe, legal speed is much safer than constantly passing.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: If there is no marked crosswalk and a pedestrian is crossing your lane, what must you do?
options: a:Slow down as you pass the pedestrian.,b:Stop and let the pedestrian finish crossing.,c:Make eye contact and then pass the pedestrian.
note: Even without a marked crosswalk, drivers must yield to pedestrians crossing their lane and allow them to finish crossing.

question: To check blind spots before changing lanes, which method should you use?
options: a:Use only the outside mirror on the side you’re moving toward.,b:Rely only on the inside rearview mirror.,c:Look over your shoulder toward the blind spot.,d:Signal and assume the lane is clear.
note: Mirrors do not show the entire area around your vehicle; there are blind spots along the sides where other vehicles can be hidden. Before changing lanes, signal and then quickly look over your shoulder in the direction you plan to move to check that blind spot, in addition to using your mirrors.

question: How can you check for vehicles in your blind spots when changing lanes?
options: a:Check the inside rearview mirror only.,b:Rely only on the outside mirrors.,c:Use the turn signal without looking.,d:Look over your left or right shoulder toward the area you cannot see in the mirrors.
note: Blind spots are areas you cannot see in your mirrors. Before changing lanes, you must briefly turn your head and look over your left or right shoulder to check these areas, while also using your mirrors and signal. This helps you see vehicles that might be hidden beside you.

question: When you see an octagonal traffic sign approaching an intersection, what must you do?
options: a:Come to a complete stop and yield as required.,b:Turn right immediately.,c:Ignore it if no other cars are present.,d:Slow down but you do not need to stop.
note: An octagonal (eight‑sided) red sign is always a STOP sign. You must come to a complete stop at the stop line, crosswalk, or before entering the intersection, then yield to pedestrians and other traffic with the right‑of‑way, and proceed only when it is safe.

question: If an oncoming vehicle doesn't dim its high beams at night, what is the best action?
options: a:Look straight ahead in your lane.,b:Look toward the left edge of the lane.,c:Look toward the right edge of your lane and use peripheral vision.
note: When an oncoming driver does not dim their high beams, looking directly at the lights can temporarily blind you. Instead, glance toward the right edge of your lane and use your peripheral vision to keep your vehicle in your lane while still watching the roadway ahead.

question: If you are on a city street and an emergency vehicle with flashing lights is behind you, what must you do?
options: a:Stay in your lane and slow down until it passes.,b:Drive to the right edge of the road and stop.,c:Drive to the right edge and slow down but not stop.
note: When an emergency vehicle approaches from behind with lights and siren on, you must pull as close as safely possible to the right edge of the road and stop, allowing it to pass. If you are in an intersection, clear the intersection first, then pull over and stop.

question: What are the consequences of refusing an alcohol analysis test when requested by law enforcement in South Dakota?
options: a:You have the right to refuse with no consequences.,b:Your driver's license will be suspended.,c:You will be fined but face no license action.,d:You will be allowed to take the test later without penalty.
note: Under implied consent laws, by driving you agree to take a chemical test if lawfully requested. In South Dakota, refusing a requested alcohol analysis test results in an administrative suspension of your driver’s license, even if you are not convicted of DUI.

question: Before starting the engine, what should you do regarding seat belts?
options: a:Buckle your safety belt and ensure passengers are buckled.,b:Buckle only if you are driving at highway speeds.,c:Tell passengers to buckle after you start driving.,d:Put on the belt after the engine is running.
note: You should always fasten your seat belt before starting the engine and make sure all passengers are buckled. This builds a consistent safety habit and ensures everyone is protected before the vehicle is in motion.

question: Which of the following is a safe driving habit?
options: a:Staring constantly at the road ahead without scanning.,b:Using high beam headlights in fog for better visibility.,c:Keeping both hands off the wheel when cruising.,d:Checking your rearview mirrors frequently to stay aware.
note: Safe drivers constantly scan the road and check mirrors to stay aware of traffic around them. This helps you spot hazards early and react in time. In fog, you should use low beams, not high beams, because high beams reflect off the fog and reduce visibility.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When preparing to make a left turn from a two-way street, where should you position your vehicle?
options: a:Near the centerline (in the lane closest to the center).,b:Near the right-hand side of the road.,c:On the left of the centerline.,d:In the right-turn-only lane.
note: For a left turn from a two‑way street, you should be in the lane closest to the centerline. Start the turn from that lane and turn into the first legal lane going in your direction, without swinging wide or cutting across lanes.

question: How should you treat an intersection with a flashing yellow traffic signal?
options: a:Slow down and proceed with caution after checking for hazards.,b:Come to a full stop then proceed, as with a stop sign.,c:Wait for a green light before moving.,d:Ignore it unless pedestrians are present.
note: A flashing yellow light means you must slow down, look for cross traffic, pedestrians, and other hazards, and proceed through the intersection with caution. You do not have to stop unless needed for safety.

question: When another driver is tailgating you, what should you do regarding the space in front of your vehicle?
options: a:Brake sharply to teach them a lesson.,b:Speed up to put distance between you and the tailgater.,c:Flash your brakes to warn the tailgater.,d:Create extra space ahead of your vehicle to reduce sudden braking risk.
note: When someone is following too closely, increase the space in front of your vehicle. A larger following distance gives you more time to brake gently and reduces the chance the tailgater will hit you if you must slow down. When safe, change lanes or let them pass.

question: Which is a common consequence of excessive speed?
options: a:It improves your ability to react to hazards.,b:It does not affect crash chances.,c:It often leads to high-risk decision-making and increases crash likelihood.
note: Excessive speed gives you less time to see and react to hazards, makes it harder to control the vehicle, and greatly increases both the chance and severity of a crash.

question: If your vehicle’s wheels have left the paved road onto the shoulder, what is the correct immediate response?
options: a:Turn sharply back onto the pavement immediately.,b:Hold the wheel steady,c:Apply full brakes and jerk the wheel to the left.,d:Speed up to try to get back on the pavement quickly.
note: If your wheels drop off the pavement, ease off the gas, hold the wheel steady, and slow down gradually. Once the car is under control and traffic allows, gently steer back onto the pavement—never jerk the wheel or brake hard.

question: If a vehicle is equipped with airbags, what should you still do?
options: a:Rely on the airbag and skip the belt.,b:Wear the seat belt behind your back.,c:Always wear your seat belt.,d:Disable the airbag to avoid injury.
note: Airbags are designed to work together with seat belts, not replace them. You should always wear your lap and shoulder belt, even in vehicles equipped with airbags.

question: What are blind spots?
options: a:Areas that cannot be seen in a vehicle’s mirrors.,b:Spots in your vision when you are tired.,c:Traffic control devices.
note: Blind spots are areas around your vehicle that you cannot see with your mirrors alone. Before changing lanes or merging, quickly look over your shoulder to check these areas.

question: If you see orange construction signs and cones on a freeway, you must:
options: a:Change lanes at full speed.,b:Slow down because the lane ends ahead always.,c:Be prepared for workers and equipment and slow down.
note: Orange signs and cones indicate a work zone. You must slow down, be alert for workers, equipment, and lane shifts, and follow any posted work-zone speed limits.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When passing on a two-lane road, what should you do first?
options: a:Flash your headlights to signal the other driver.,b:Sound your horn as you pass.,c:Judge the distance and speed of any oncoming vehicles.
note: Before passing on a two-lane road, you must first make sure it is safe by judging the distance and speed of oncoming vehicles and the vehicle you are passing. Only when you are certain you have enough clear space should you move into the opposing lane. Flashing headlights or sounding the horn is not a required first step and is not a substitute for checking that you have enough time and distance.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: What important action should you take before making a turn?
options: a:Increase your speed to complete the turn faster.,b:Always move to the left lane before turning.,c:Check traffic in all directions.
note: Before making any turn, you must check traffic in all directions—ahead, behind, and to both sides—using your mirrors and turning your head as needed. This ensures you do not cut off other vehicles, bicycles, or pedestrians. Increasing speed or automatically moving to the left lane is unsafe and not required unless the turn itself specifically requires a lane change that is done safely and in advance.

question: When you see a reflective orange triangle on a vehicle's rear, it means:
options: a:The vehicle is slow-moving (usually 25 mph or less).,b:The vehicle is an ambulance.,c:The vehicle is a school bus.
note: A reflective orange triangle on the rear of a vehicle is the slow-moving vehicle emblem. It warns that the vehicle usually travels at 25 mph or less, such as farm equipment or certain construction vehicles. It does not indicate an ambulance or school bus.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: How is a crosswalk defined?
options: a:A name for a four-way intersection.,b:The area where pedestrians are allowed to cross the roadway.,c:An area set aside for road workers.,d:A place where vehicles always have the right-of-way.
note: A crosswalk is the part of the roadway set aside for pedestrians to cross, whether it is painted (marked) or exists legally at an intersection even without painted lines (unmarked). Drivers must yield to pedestrians in crosswalks; vehicles do not automatically have the right-of-way there.

question: A long truck turning right may appear to do what on a two-lane street?
options: a:Complete the turn strictly within the right lane.,b:Finish the turn in either of the two available lanes without swing.,c:Swing wide to complete the turn.
note: Long trucks and other large vehicles often need to swing wide to the left before turning right because their rear wheels follow a shorter, tighter path than the front wheels. Drivers behind or beside these trucks should not try to squeeze into the space the truck leaves while swinging wide, as the truck will need that space to complete the turn safely.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When parking uphill on a two-way road with no curb, which way should you turn your front wheels?
options: a:Toward the edge of the road (right) so the vehicle will roll away from the center.,b:Straight ahead so it won’t roll.,c:Toward the center of the road (left) so it will roll into traffic.,d:Any direction is acceptable as long as you set the parking brake.
note: On an uphill road with no curb, turn your front wheels toward the edge of the road. If your brakes fail, the vehicle will roll off the roadway instead of into oncoming traffic.

question: If you are in an intersection when an emergency vehicle with lights and siren is approaching, what must you do?
options: a:Pull to the right of the intersection and stop immediately.,b:Continue through the intersection,c:Stop immediately in the intersection until it passes.
note: If you are already in an intersection when an emergency vehicle approaches, continue through and clear the intersection first. Then, as soon as it is safe, pull to the right side of the road and stop to let the emergency vehicle pass.

question: If you intend to pass a pedestrian and an oncoming vehicle is approaching, what should you do?
options: a:Honk to warn the pedestrian to move over.,b:Keep your speed and pass the pedestrian quickly.,c:Slow down and allow the oncoming vehicle to pass first.
note: When you must pass a pedestrian and there is oncoming traffic, slow down and let the oncoming vehicle pass first. This gives you more space and time so you can move around the pedestrian safely without crowding them or the oncoming lane.

question: What is the effect of slowing down just to look at collisions or unusual events?
options: a:It causes traffic congestion and can lead to further collisions.,b:It improves traffic flow by reducing speed variability.,c:It prevents rear-end collisions by encouraging slower traffic.,d:It is required by law to slow and observe.
note: Slowing down just to look at a crash or something unusual, called rubbernecking, disrupts traffic flow and can cause sudden braking and rear-end collisions. Stay focused on the road ahead and keep moving at a safe, steady speed.

question: Why is extra space needed in front of a large truck?
options: a:Because trucks always drive slower than cars.,b:To allow other drivers to merge in front of the truck.,c:So the truck has room to stop safely.,d:To give the truck room to turn more easily.
note: Large trucks need much more distance to stop because of their size and weight. Leaving extra space in front of a truck gives the driver enough room to brake safely and helps prevent rear-end collisions if traffic slows suddenly.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: If a traffic signal at an intersection turns steady yellow before you reach it, what should you do if you haven't entered the intersection?
options: a:Speed up to clear the intersection before it turns red.,b:Proceed through at the same speed.,c:Come to a safe stop.
note: A steady yellow light means the signal is about to turn red. If you have not yet entered the intersection, you are expected to slow down and stop if you can do so safely. Only continue through if a sudden stop would be unsafe, such as if someone is following too closely behind you.

question: What is a good way to avoid skidding on slick surfaces?
options: a:Slow down before entering curves and intersections.,b:Speed up before entering a curve and slow down exiting it.,c:Shift into a lower gear after starting down a steep hill.
note: On wet, icy, or otherwise slick roads, you are more likely to skid if you brake or turn suddenly. Slow down before you enter curves and intersections so you can steer and brake gently through them, which helps your tires maintain traction.

question: After stopping for a train at a railroad crossing and the train passes, what should you do before proceeding?
options: a:Wait until the signal lights stop flashing.,b:Proceed immediately when the train has passed if the track looks clear.,c:Roll forward slowly to check for tracks.,d:Both wait for the signals to stop and look for a second train.
note: After a train passes, another train may be approaching on a different track. Stay stopped until all gates are fully raised and all warning lights and bells have stopped. Then look and listen carefully in both directions for a second train before crossing.

question: If the centerline has one solid yellow and one broken yellow line next to your lane, what does that mean?
options: a:You are not allowed to pass here.,b:You are in a passing zone and may pass on the left when clear.,c:You may only make right turns here.
note: A solid yellow line means no passing from that side; a broken yellow line means passing is allowed when safe. If the broken yellow line is next to your lane, you may cross it to pass another vehicle when the way is clear. Drivers on the solid-line side may not pass.

question: As your speed increases, what becomes more important?
options: a:Turning on headlights.,b:Changing lanes frequently to keep flow.,c:Looking well ahead of your vehicle.
note: The faster you drive, the longer it takes to see a hazard, react, and stop. Looking well ahead of your vehicle at higher speeds gives you more time and space to adjust your speed or position and avoid sudden, unsafe maneuvers.

question: Before returning to your lane after overtaking another vehicle, what should you confirm?
options: a:You can see both headlights of the passed vehicle in your rearview mirror.,b:You have flashed your headlights.,c:You are travelling at the same speed as before the pass.,d:You have sounded your horn to signal your return.
note: After passing, don’t move back too soon. Wait until you can see both headlights of the vehicle you passed clearly in your interior rearview mirror. That means you’ve created enough space so you can return to your lane without cutting the other driver off or forcing them to brake suddenly.

question: Which road surface tends to freeze first?
options: a:A bridge,b:A tunnel,c:An intersection
note: Bridges and overpasses freeze first because cold air flows both above and below the surface, causing the pavement to lose heat faster than regular roads. Even when the main roadway looks just wet, a bridge can be icy and very slippery, so you should slow down and avoid sudden braking or steering.

question: Which action helps reduce incidents of road rage?
options: a:Talk on your cell phone to stay calm.,b:Use your horn frequently to motivate other drivers.,c:Tailgate slower drivers to express frustration.,d:Always signal before changing lanes.
note: To reduce road rage, drive predictably and courteously. Always signaling before changing lanes lets other drivers know what you plan to do, giving them time to adjust and reducing surprise or anger. Avoid aggressive behaviors like tailgating, frequent horn use, or distracted driving, which can escalate tensions on the road.

question: Which headlights should you use to improve visibility in rain or fog?
options: a:Hazard flashers only.,b:High beam headlights.,c:Parking lights.,d:Low beam headlights.
note: In rain, fog, or snow, use low beam headlights. High beams reflect off moisture droplets in the air and can shine back into your eyes, making it harder to see and also creating more glare for other drivers. Low beams cut under the fog and improve your ability to see the road and be seen by others.

question: Where is the safest place for children aged 12 and under to ride in a vehicle with airbags?
options: a:In the bed of a pickup truck.,b:In the front seat.,c:In the back seat.
note: Children 12 and under should ride in the back seat, properly restrained in an appropriate child safety seat or booster as required by their age, height, and weight. Front airbags are designed for adults and can deploy with great force, which can seriously injure or kill a child in the front seat during a crash.

question: If a tire suddenly goes flat while driving, what should you do first?
options: a:Rapidly pump the brake pedal several times.,b:Grip the wheel firmly,c:Brake as hard as you can immediately.
note: If a tire blows out, keep a firm grip on the steering wheel and hold it straight so you maintain control. Take your foot off the accelerator and let the vehicle slow down gradually. Once you have the car under control and your speed has dropped, brake gently if needed and move off the road to a safe place.

question: What should you do if the road is wet or icy?
options: a:Reduce your speed to improve traction.,b:Drive at the posted speed limit regardless.,c:Turn off your headlights to reduce glare.,d:Increase your speed to get through the hazard quickly.
note: On wet, snowy, or icy roads, your tires have less grip, so it takes longer to stop and is easier to skid. You must reduce your speed below the posted limit and drive smoothly, allowing extra space to stop. The posted speed limit is for ideal conditions, not for bad weather.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Which statement about blind spots is true?
options: a:Blind spots can be seen using only the rearview mirror.,b:Blind spots are eliminated if you have one outside mirror.,c:Large trucks have bigger blind spots than most passenger vehicles.
note: Blind spots are areas you cannot see in your mirrors and must check by turning your head. All vehicles have blind spots, but large trucks and buses have much larger ones on all sides. Because of this, you should avoid lingering alongside or close behind large trucks where the driver may not see you.

question: Double solid yellow centerlines indicate that passing is:
options: a:Not allowed from either direction.,b:Allowed only from your direction of travel.,c:Allowed from both directions.,d:Allowed only during daylight hours.
note: Double solid yellow centerlines separate traffic moving in opposite directions and mean that passing is not allowed from either direction. You may cross them only when making a permitted left turn or when instructed by traffic control, but not to pass another vehicle.

question: When approaching a pedestrian using a white cane or guide dog, what must you do?
options: a:Carefully drive around them.,b:Honk your horn to warn them as you pass.,c:Stop and remain stopped until the person is clear of your path.
note: A pedestrian using a white cane or guide dog is visually impaired and has the right-of-way. You must stop and remain stopped until the person has completely crossed your lane and is clear of your path. Do not honk or drive around them, as this can be confusing and dangerous.

question: Accumulating how many points on your driving record within 24 months will lead to license suspension in South Dakota?
options: a:15 points,b:30 points,c:22 points
note: South Dakota uses a point system to track traffic violations. If you accumulate 22 or more points within a 24‑month period, your driver’s license will be suspended. The more points you have, the longer the suspension can be, so avoiding repeated violations is important to keep your driving privilege.

question: When merging onto a freeway, at what speed should you enter traffic?
options: a:Enter at or near the speed of freeway traffic.,b:Enter five to ten mph slower than freeway traffic.,c:Enter at the posted speed limit regardless of traffic flow.
note: When using a freeway on‑ramp, you should use the acceleration lane to reach a speed that matches the flow of freeway traffic, as long as it is safe and not above the speed limit. Entering much slower than other vehicles forces them to brake or swerve and increases the risk of a collision.

question: When must you yield to a pedestrian using a white cane or guide dog?
options: a:Only when the guide dog is actively leading them across the street.,b:Only if a crossing guard is present.,c:At all times.
note: A person using a white cane or a guide dog is visually impaired and is given special right‑of‑way protection. You must always yield to them, stop if necessary, and allow them to cross safely, regardless of whether a crossing guard is present or whether the dog appears to be actively leading.

question: How can you best monitor traffic behind your vehicle?
options: a:Rely only on side mirrors.,b:Turn and look out your back window periodically.,c:Frequently check your rearview mirror.,d:Keep other vehicles out of your blind spots at all times.
note: To stay aware of traffic behind you, check your inside rearview mirror frequently—about every few seconds in normal driving. This helps you notice vehicles that are following too closely, approaching quickly, or preparing to pass, so you can adjust your speed or lane position safely.

question: Which habit is especially dangerous in work zones?
options: a:Both of the above.,b:Failing to watch for workers and moving equipment.,c:Tailgating another vehicle.
note: Work zones often have narrowed lanes, changing traffic patterns, and workers close to moving vehicles. Tailgating reduces your time to react if traffic slows suddenly, and failing to watch for workers and equipment can lead to serious crashes. You should slow down, increase following distance, and stay alert for workers and machinery.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: When entering the interstate, after matching the speed of traffic and signaling, what should you do?
options: a:Stop on the ramp until a vehicle makes room.,b:Merge carefully into the gap.,c:Wait for the lane to clear completely before merging.,d:Expect traffic to allow you to proceed because you have the right-of-way.
note: On an interstate entrance ramp, use the acceleration lane to reach the speed of traffic, signal, find a safe gap, and then merge smoothly into that gap. Do not stop on the ramp unless absolutely necessary, and never assume other drivers must yield to you.

question: When driving near a large commercial vehicle, what is a safe practice?
options: a:Follow closely to reduce wind drag.,b:Drive on its right side when on curves and hills.,c:Avoid driving alongside it for long stretches because of its large blind spots.,d:Pass safely and promptly rather than lingering beside the truck.
note: Large trucks and buses have extensive blind spots on both sides, especially on the right. Avoid driving alongside them for long periods so the driver can see you and you have room to react if the truck changes lanes or needs to maneuver suddenly.

question: When a car with bright headlights approaches you at night, how should you respond?
options: a:Stop until the other driver passes.,b:Flash your high beams at them.,c:Glance toward the right edge of your lane to avoid being blinded.,d:Look directly at their headlights to judge distance.
note: Bright oncoming headlights can temporarily blind you. Keep your eyes toward the right edge of your lane or the right side of the road to use it as a guide, and avoid looking directly into the other vehicle’s lights.

question: What is the purpose of broken yellow lines on streets and highways?
options: a:Indicate no passing zones.,b:Separate lanes moving in the same direction.,c:Separate lanes of traffic moving in opposite directions and allow passing.
note: Yellow lines separate traffic moving in opposite directions. When the yellow line is broken (dashed), you may pass another vehicle if it is safe and legal, with enough clear distance ahead.

question: What should you do to reduce traction loss on wet roads?
options: a:Turn off electronic stability control.,b:Slow down and avoid abrupt turns or braking.,c:Make sharp turns to maintain control.,d:Apply brakes firmly at the first sign of sliding.
note: On wet roads, slow down and make all steering, accelerating, and braking actions gentle and gradual. Lower speed and smooth inputs help your tires maintain grip and reduce the risk of skidding or hydroplaning.

question: When is a collision more likely to occur relative to traffic flow?
options: a:When all vehicles travel at similar speeds.,b:When one lane is slightly faster than another.,c:When one vehicle is traveling significantly faster or slower than the flow.
note: Collisions are more likely when one vehicle is moving much faster or much slower than surrounding traffic. Large speed differences increase lane changes, passing, and braking conflicts, which raises the risk of rear‑end and side‑impact crashes. When most vehicles travel at similar speeds, there are fewer conflicts and generally lower crash risk.

question: Which is the correct behavior when driving through a work zone?
options: a:Maintain your normal speed the whole way through.,b:Weave between cones to get ahead of traffic.,c:Increase speed to clear the zone quickly.,d:Reduce speed
note: In work zones you must slow down, obey the posted work‑zone speed limit, and be prepared to stop suddenly. Workers, equipment, and lane shifts can appear unexpectedly, so reducing speed and driving cautiously is essential for safety and is required by law in all states.

question: What does a yellow left-turn arrow in a traffic signal indicate?
options: a:Drivers should prepare to yield only to oncoming traffic.,b:Wait four seconds before proceeding.,c:The protected left-turn phase is ending and you must prepare to yield.
note: A yellow left‑turn arrow means your protected left‑turn phase is ending. If you are already in the intersection, complete the turn carefully. If you have not yet entered, prepare to stop and be ready to yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians, because the signal will soon change and you may lose the protected turn.

question: What are "no zones" around large trucks?
options: a:Only the space directly behind the truck.,b:Areas where cars disappear into blind spots or are so close they restrict the truck's ability to stop or maneuver.,c:Designated safe passing zones.,d:Areas where cars have several car lengths between their vehicle and the truck.
note: No‑zones are the large blind spots and danger areas around trucks and other large vehicles. If you drive in these areas, the truck driver may not see you, or you may be so close that the truck cannot stop or maneuver safely. Stay out of these zones by avoiding lingering alongside trucks and by not following too closely.

question: Interstate driving requires drivers to:
options: a:Only be able to drive at higher speeds.,b:Relax because highways are safer.,c:Be constantly alert and have the ability to safely drive at increased speeds.
note: Interstate driving involves higher speeds, heavier traffic, and more complex merging and lane‑changing. Drivers must stay constantly alert, scan far ahead, and be able to control their vehicle smoothly at increased speeds to enter, exit, and adjust to traffic safely.

question: Before changing lanes, besides checking mirrors, what else should you do?
options: a:Never look over your right shoulder.,b:Glance over your shoulder to check your blind spot.,c:Always slow down in your lane.,d:Honk to let others know you are moving.
note: Before changing lanes, check your mirrors and then quickly glance over your shoulder in the direction you plan to move. This shoulder check lets you see the blind spot that mirrors cannot cover, helping you avoid vehicles, motorcycles, or bicycles that may be alongside you.

question: What does a solid yellow line beside a broken yellow line mean for drivers next to the broken line?
options: a:Traffic next to the solid line may pass when safe.,b:Both directions may pass.,c:Traffic next to the broken line may pass when safe.,d:Neither direction may pass.
note: A solid yellow line next to a broken yellow line means only the traffic on the side with the broken line may cross the center line to pass when it is safe. Drivers on the side with the solid line must not pass because it is considered unsafe from that direction.

question: If you see pedestrians in an upcoming crosswalk, what should you do?
options: a:Continue ahead because you have the right-of-way.,b:Pull to the right and go around the pedestrians.,c:Sound your horn and proceed quickly.,d:Wait for the pedestrians to finish crossing.
note: Drivers must yield to pedestrians in a crosswalk and wait until the intersection is clear before proceeding.

question: If you begin to feel tired while driving, what should you do?
options: a:Drink something with caffeine and keep going.,b:Stop and either rest or switch drivers.,c:Reduce speed and continue driving.,d:Open a window for fresh air.
note: If you feel tired while driving, the safe choice is to stop and rest or switch drivers. Drowsy driving greatly reduces your reaction time and judgment, and short-term tricks like opening a window or drinking caffeine are not reliable substitutes for real rest.

question: When is it necessary to use low beam headlights?
options: a:Any time you are in fog.,b:Only when parked at night.,c:Only on a lighted street.,d:Only on a freeway.
note: In fog, you should use low beam headlights because high beams reflect off the water droplets in the air and can make it harder to see. Low beams provide better forward visibility and help other drivers see you without creating extra glare.

question: If someone is tailgating you on a two-lane road and there's no lane to move into, what should you do?
options: a:Slow down gradually to encourage the tailgater to pass.,b:Speed up to increase distance from them.,c:Apply your brakes sharply to warn them.
note: If someone is following too closely and you cannot safely change lanes, the safest response is to gradually reduce your speed when it is safe. This increases the space in front of you, giving you more time to react if something happens ahead, and often encourages the tailgater to pass when there is an opportunity. Never slam on your brakes or speed up, as both can increase the risk of a collision.

question: Which behavior most blocks smooth traffic flow?
options: a:Using public transportation instead of driving.,b:Avoiding unnecessary lane changes.,c:Slowing down to look at a collision scene (rubbernecking).,d:Signaling every lane change.
note: Slowing down to look at a collision or roadside incident, known as rubbernecking, is a major cause of traffic slowdowns and can lead to additional crashes. It disrupts the smooth flow of traffic because drivers unnecessarily reduce speed and divert their attention from the road. You should keep your eyes on the road ahead and maintain a safe, steady speed unless you are required to slow or stop.

question: Why should you keep your turn signal on continuously while you are turning?
options: a:Signal continuously so other road users know your intentions.,b:Turning signals are only necessary when changing lanes.,c:Keeping it on makes the turn faster.,d:Because it's illegal to switch off your signal before completing the turn.
note: You should keep your turn signal on throughout the entire turn or lane change so that other drivers, cyclists, and pedestrians clearly understand what you are doing. Signaling early and continuously until the maneuver is complete helps others adjust their speed and position, reducing the chance of collisions. Turn signals are required for turns and lane changes, not to make the vehicle turn faster.

question: Accumulating how many points on your license within 12 months can result in suspension in South Dakota?
options: a:Ten points.,b:Eight points.,c:Fifteen points.
note: In South Dakota, accumulating 15 or more points within a 12-month period can lead to license suspension; penalties vary by offense count.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: If you plan to pass another vehicle, which assumption is unsafe?
options: a:Not assuming the other driver will make space for you to return.,b:Assuming other drivers will maintain a constant speed.,c:Assuming the other driver will make room for you because you signaled.
note: When passing, you must never assume that other drivers will slow down, move over, or make room for you just because you signaled. Always base your decision to pass on actual traffic conditions: available space, sight distance, and the speed of oncoming traffic. Signaling communicates your intention, but it does not give you the right‑of‑way or guarantee that others will cooperate.

question: When following a large truck on the freeway, how much space should you maintain?
options: a:More distance than you would behind a passenger vehicle.,b:Directly beside the truck to pass quicker.,c:As close as possible to use their slipstream.,d:One car length behind so the truck driver can see you.
note: When following a large truck, leave more space than you would behind a passenger car. Trucks block your view of the road ahead and need more distance to stop. Extra following distance gives you more time to react and helps you stay out of the truck driver’s blind spots.

question: When following a motorcycle, you should:
options: a:Be ready to use your horn.,b:Allow a larger following distance.,c:Share the lane with the motorcycle.,d:Drive more slowly directly behind the motorcycle.
note: Motorcycles can stop, swerve, or lose traction more quickly than cars, so you should allow at least a three‑ to four‑second following distance. This extra space gives you time to react if the rider brakes or swerves suddenly and helps prevent rear‑end collisions.

question: You are exiting the freeway on a downhill ramp that curves. What should you do?
options: a:Wait until you are in the curve to begin braking.,b:Slow to the posted speed limit of the freeway first.,c:Slow to a safe speed before entering the curve.
note: On a downhill, curving exit ramp, you should slow to a safe speed before you enter the curve. Braking hard while already in the curve, especially going downhill, can cause skidding and loss of control. Enter the curve at a controlled speed, then steer smoothly through it.

question: If the driver ahead of you stops at a crosswalk, what should you do?
options: a:Cautiously pass the vehicle at 10 mph or slower.,b:Stop and wait until all pedestrians have crossed before proceeding.,c:Change lanes and pass the stopped vehicle.,d:Sound your horn to make the driver move on.
note: Do not pass a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk; pedestrians may be crossing that you cannot see.

question: How should you adjust speed and steering when driving on snowy or icy roads?
options: a:Brake suddenly to test traction.,b:Drive the same as under normal conditions.,c:Use cruise control to maintain a steady speed.,d:Make speed and directional changes more gradually than usual.
note: On snowy or icy roads, make all speed and steering changes more gradually than usual. Sudden braking, acceleration, or sharp steering can cause your tires to lose traction and the vehicle to skid. Avoid cruise control and drive smoothly to maintain control.

question: What are the standard colors for temporary construction or maintenance signs?
options: a:White background with red letters.,b:Orange background with black letters or symbols.,c:Red background with green letters.,d:Yellow background with blue letters.
note: Temporary construction and maintenance signs are standardized with an orange background and black letters or symbols. The bright orange color alerts drivers to work zones and changing road conditions so they can slow down and proceed with extra caution.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Which passing actions are unlawful?
options: a:Passing on the right when multiple lanes are present.,b:Passing on hills and curves where you cannot see far enough ahead.,c:Passing in any marked no-passing zone, at or near a railroad crossing, or where solid lines indicate no passing.,d:Passing during daylight in rural areas.
note: Passing is illegal in any marked no‑passing zone, at or near railroad crossings, on hills or curves where you cannot see far enough ahead, and anywhere a solid line on your side of the road indicates no passing. These restrictions exist because oncoming traffic or hazards may be hidden, leaving you without enough distance to pass safely.

question: While driving at night, what should you do to compensate for reduced visibility?
options: a:Look directly into the headlights of oncoming vehicles.,b:Always use your high beams.,c:Increase your following distance.
note: At night you cannot see as far ahead, so you should increase your following distance to give yourself more time to react to hazards. Use your headlights properly and avoid looking directly into oncoming headlights so you are not blinded and can keep a clear view of the road.

question: If a tire suddenly blows out while driving, what is the correct action?
options: a:Brake hard and steer to the right edge of the roadway.,b:Grip the steering wheel firmly, slow down, and exit the traffic lane.,c:Pump the brakes rapidly to stop quickly.
note: If a tire blows out, hold the steering wheel firmly to keep control, ease off the accelerator, and let the vehicle slow down gradually. Do not brake hard; instead, when the vehicle has slowed and you have control, gently apply the brakes as needed and steer to a safe place out of the traffic lane.

question: Why should you avoid making sudden stops in front of large trucks and buses?
options: a:Large trucks always travel faster than small vehicles.,b:Trucks can brake quicker due to advanced braking systems.,c:Large trucks and buses need longer distances to stop than smaller vehicles.,d:Drivers of small cars can’t see trucks in their mirrors.
note: Large trucks and buses are much heavier than passenger cars, so they need a longer distance to come to a complete stop. If you make a sudden stop in front of them, they may not be able to slow down in time, increasing the risk of a rear‑end collision.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: A pedestrian who begins crossing after the 'Don't Walk' signal is flashing is mid-crossing when your light turns green. What must you do?
options: a:Proceed if you have the right-of-way.,b:Proceed if the pedestrian is not in your lane.,c:Wait until the pedestrian finishes crossing before proceeding.
note: You must yield to any pedestrian already in the crosswalk; wait for them to clear the roadway before moving on your green.

question: Approaching an intersection with a flashing yellow light, what must you do?
options: a:Slow down and proceed with caution.,b:Come to a complete stop at the intersection.,c:Accelerate to get through quickly.,d:Maintain your normal speed.
note: A flashing yellow light means you do not have to stop, but you must slow down and proceed with extra caution. Be prepared to yield and watch carefully for cross traffic, pedestrians, or hazards in the intersection.

question: Which statement best describes how defensive drivers think?
options: a:They consider what other drivers might do and are prepared to react.,b:They assume other drivers will always do the right thing.,c:They expect no breaks and give none.,d:They rely solely on traffic signals for safety.
note: Defensive drivers constantly scan the road and think about what other drivers, cyclists, and pedestrians might do next. They anticipate possible mistakes by others and are ready to slow, stop, or change lanes to avoid a collision.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: If the intersection ahead is blocked by traffic but your light is green, what should you do?
options: a:Stay out of the intersection until traffic clears.,b:Follow other vehicles into the intersection so you don't delay.,c:Turn left to find an alternate route immediately.
note: Even with a green light, you must not enter an intersection unless there is enough space to clear it completely. If traffic ahead is stopped and would leave you blocking the intersection, you must wait behind the stop line until it clears.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Which is the correct method for checking blind spots when changing lanes?
options: a:Look over your right shoulder for a right lane change and your left shoulder for a left lane change.,b:You only need to turn and look over your right shoulder for all lane changes.,c:Vehicles with two outside mirrors do not have blind spots.
note: Before changing lanes, signal, check your mirrors, and then quickly look over the shoulder on the side you are moving toward. This head check lets you see into the blind spot that mirrors cannot cover.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Drivers turning left must yield to which vehicles?
options: a:No one; they have the right-of-way.,b:Only pedestrians.,c:Vehicles overtaking from behind.,d:Oncoming cars.
note: When turning left, you must yield to oncoming traffic that is going straight or turning right, as well as to pedestrians in the crosswalk. Oncoming vehicles have the right-of-way because they are continuing straight through the intersection, while you are crossing their path.

question: A broken yellow centerline next to your lane means what?
options: a:Passing on the left is permitted when the way ahead is clear.,b:Passing is not permitted.,c:Passing on the left is permitted when the way ahead is clear.,d:Passing rules cannot be determined from this marking.
note: A broken yellow centerline means passing is allowed on the left when it is safe and there is no oncoming traffic. Yellow lines separate traffic moving in opposite directions, and you may only cross them to pass another vehicle or turn left when the way ahead is clear.

question: What is the purpose of barriers, drums, cones, and signs in work zones?
options: a:To inconvenience drivers and slow traffic intentionally.,b:To provide decorative separation only.,c:To keep traffic out of hazardous areas and direct travel safely.,d:To make drivers angry about slowdowns.
note: Barriers, drums, cones, and signs in work zones are used to guide drivers safely through or around construction areas and to keep vehicles out of hazardous zones. They protect both drivers and workers by clearly marking lane changes, closed areas, and reduced-speed sections.

question: What is a common effect of continuous hard braking on icy or snowy roads?
options: a:It increases tire traction on ice.,b:It helps you stop faster in slippery conditions.,c:It often locks the front wheels,d:It keeps your brakes from freezing.
note: On icy or snowy roads, continuous hard braking can cause your wheels—especially the front wheels—to lock. When the wheels lock, you lose steering control and may skid. Instead, slow down early, brake gently, and if your vehicle has ABS, apply firm, steady pressure so the system can prevent wheel lockup.

question: If you see animals standing near the roadway, what should you do?
options: a:Quickly swerve into the next lane.,b:Speed up to scare them away.,c:Slow down and proceed with caution.,d:Stop and get out of your vehicle to move them.
note: If animals are near the roadway, slow down and be prepared to stop. Animals can move unpredictably or be followed by others you do not see yet. Reducing speed and proceeding with caution gives you more time to react and helps avoid sudden swerves that could cause a crash.

question: If your vehicle begins to skid, what is the correct action to take?
options: a:Ease off the gas and steer in the direction of the skid.,b:Accelerate to regain traction.,c:Turn off the ignition immediately.,d:Brake as hard as possible.
note: When a vehicle begins to skid, sudden braking or acceleration can make the skid worse. You should gently ease off the accelerator (and off the brake if you were braking) and steer in the direction you want the front of the vehicle to go, which is generally the same direction the rear of the vehicle is skidding. This helps the tires regain traction and allows you to gradually regain control.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: If you miss your freeway exit, what should you do?
options: a:Stop immediately and reverse to the exit.,b:Back up on the shoulder to reach the exit.,c:Cross the median to return to your exit.,d:Continue to the next exit and re-route; do not back up.
note: If you miss your freeway exit, you must never stop, back up, or cross the median on the freeway. These actions are extremely dangerous and illegal in most jurisdictions. Instead, continue to the next exit, leave the freeway safely, and then re-route using surface streets or by re-entering the freeway in the opposite direction if needed.

question: If you damage a parked vehicle and cannot find the owner, what must you do?
options: a:Call your insurance company when you get home without leaving a note.,b:Drive away and report it later to the police.,c:Leave a note with your name, contact information, and an explanation of the accident, and report it if required.,d:Wait by the car until the owner returns.
note: If you hit a parked vehicle and cannot find the owner, you are legally required to stop and leave a clearly visible note with your name, contact information, and an explanation of the accident. In many states you must also promptly report the collision to law enforcement. Leaving the scene without providing information is considered a hit-and-run, which is a serious offense.

question: What can happen if you take a prescription drug and drink alcohol?
options: a:It will improve alertness.,b:It will likely have no effect.,c:It can make you unfit to drive.,d:It can increase impairment and make driving dangerous.
note: Combining alcohol with prescription or over‑the‑counter drugs can greatly increase drowsiness, slow reaction time, and affect judgment. Even if each substance alone might not make you feel very impaired, together they can make you unsafe and legally unfit to drive. Always check medication labels and consult your doctor or pharmacist before driving after taking any drug, especially if you also drink alcohol.

question: What should you remove from your vehicle before driving in winter conditions?
options: a:Only the windshield and passenger window.,b:Only the front windshield so you can see ahead.,c:Just clear the headlights and taillights.,d:All snow, ice, and frost from windows, mirrors, lights, and the roof.
note: Before driving in winter conditions, you must clear all snow, ice, and frost from your vehicle, including all windows, mirrors, lights, and the roof. Full visibility in every direction is essential for safe driving, and snow left on the roof can slide onto your windshield or blow off and endanger other road users.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Whose directions must drivers obey at construction sites?
options: a:Security guards patrolling parking lots.,b:Bystanders waving their hands.,c:Drivers with broken-down vehicles asking you to stop.,d:Flaggers (signal persons) directing traffic.
note: Flaggers (also called signal persons) are authorized to control traffic in construction and work zones. Their directions override normal traffic signals and signs while they are on duty, and drivers must obey their instructions to protect workers and other road users.

question: If driving next to a single broken white line on a highway, what may you do?
options: a:You may cross only if you are in the left lane.,b:You cannot cross the line to pass.,c:You may cross the line to pass or change lanes if it is safe.
note: A single broken white line separates lanes of traffic moving in the same direction. You may cross a broken white line to change lanes or pass another vehicle when it is safe and legal to do so, after checking mirrors and blind spots and signaling.

question: When entering or exiting a driveway, what should drivers do regarding pedestrians?
options: a:Honk at pedestrians to make them yield.,b:Proceed without stopping if no vehicle is approaching.,c:Have the right-of-way over pedestrians.,d:Yield to pedestrians and stop before entering the sidewalk area.
note: When entering or exiting a driveway or alley, you must stop before crossing the sidewalk area and yield to pedestrians on the sidewalk. Pedestrians using the sidewalk have the right-of-way, and you may proceed only after the sidewalk is clear and it is safe.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: Where is it legal to pass another vehicle?
options: a:On a curve if no oncoming vehicles are visible.,b:In any lane if traffic ahead is slow.,c:Only where signs or pavement markings allow overtaking.,d:Within an intersection if you don’t see oncoming traffic.
note: Passing is only legal where signs and pavement markings allow it, such as where there is a broken center line and no prohibitory signs. Even then, you may pass only if you have enough clear distance ahead, good visibility, and can complete the maneuver safely without exceeding the speed limit.

question: What do double solid yellow lane markings mean?
options: a:The lane to the right may pass.,b:Both directions may pass when clear.,c:Neither direction may pass.
note: Double solid yellow lines separate traffic moving in opposite directions and mean that passing is not allowed from either direction. You must stay in your lane and may not cross these lines to pass, except in limited situations such as turning left into or out of a driveway or side road where state law allows.

question: At a red traffic light with a green arrow, when may you proceed in the arrow's direction?
options: a:Only after coming to a complete stop first.,b:Only if no other vehicles are present.,c:When you are in the proper lane and the roadway is clear.,d:Only after the arrow turns off.
note: A green arrow is a protected movement signal. When you are in the correct lane and the path is clear of vehicles, pedestrians, and hazards, you may proceed in the direction of the arrow without stopping, even though the circular red light is on.

question: Why is using a cell phone while driving a distraction?
options: a:It occupies the driver's hands, eyes, and mind.,b:It causes the driver to worry about call costs.,c:It draws other drivers’ attention away from the road.
note: Using a cell phone while driving is dangerous because it takes your eyes off the road, your hands off the wheel, and your mind off driving. This combination greatly increases the chance of missing hazards and being involved in a crash.

question: If the rear of your vehicle begins skidding left, how should you steer?
options: a:Turn the steering wheel left in the direction of the skid.,b:Brake hard immediately.,c:Do not turn the steering wheel at all.,d:Turn sharply right to counter the skid.
note: If the rear of your vehicle skids left, you should ease off the accelerator and steer left, in the same direction the rear is sliding. Steering into the skid helps the wheels realign with the direction of travel so you can regain traction and control. Avoid hard braking, which can make the skid worse.

question: A solid yellow line on your side of the centerline indicates what?
options: a:Reduce your speed.,b:Do not pass.,c:Traffic light ahead.,d:Pass only during daylight hours.
note: A solid yellow line on your side of the centerline means you must not pass another vehicle in your lane. If there is a solid line next to a broken yellow line, only traffic on the side with the broken line is allowed to pass when it is safe.

question: If your vehicle starts to skid, what is the recommended initial response?
options: a:Pump the brakes repeatedly.,b:Brake abruptly to stop the skid.,c:Stay off the brakes and steer to regain control.
note: When your vehicle begins to skid, your first response should be to stay off the brakes and off the accelerator. Sudden braking can lock the wheels and make the skid worse. Instead, look where you want to go and steer smoothly in that direction to help the tires regain traction.

question: If weather or light conditions require headlights, which should you use?
options: a:Emergency flashers only.,b:Low beam headlights.,c:High beam headlights.,d:Parking lights only.
note: In rain, fog, snow, or low light, you should use low beam headlights. High beams can reflect off moisture or fog and actually make it harder to see. Emergency flashers and parking lights alone are not a substitute for proper headlights when visibility is reduced.

question: Who may legally use designated handicap parking spaces?
options: a:Anyone if all other spaces are full.,b:People who feel unwell even without a placard.,c:Delivery drivers unloading packages temporarily.,d:Only drivers with the appropriate license plate or hang tag.
note: Designated handicap (accessible) parking spaces are reserved for people with disabilities who have and display the proper license plate or placard issued under state law. Others may not use these spaces, even briefly or if they feel unwell, unless transporting the person to whom the placard or plate is issued.

question: What is distracted driving?
options: a:Only using a cellphone while driving.,b:Anything that causes evasive action while driving.,c:Anything that causes you to pay more attention to driving.,d:Anything that takes your attention away from driving.
note: Distracted driving is any activity that takes your attention away from driving. This includes visual distractions (eyes off the road), manual distractions (hands off the wheel), and cognitive distractions (mind off driving), such as texting, eating, or adjusting controls.

question: When parking on any hill, what should you always do?
options: a:Have one rear wheel touch the curb.,b:Keep your front wheels parallel to the road even if there's no curb.,c:Use your parking brake and leave the vehicle in park or in gear.
note: When parking on any hill, always set the parking brake and leave the vehicle in park (automatic) or in gear (manual) so it does not roll. In addition, you should turn your wheels appropriately for uphill or downhill parking, but using the parking brake and securing the transmission is always required.

question: When you encounter a flashing red traffic light, you must:
options: a:Proceed only after it turns green.,b:Treat the intersection as if it were controlled by a stop sign.,c:Yield only to traffic on your left.,d:Are traveling in the wrong direction.
note: A flashing red traffic light means you must come to a complete stop, just as you would at a stop sign. After stopping, yield to any traffic or pedestrians with the right-of-way, then proceed through the intersection only when it is safe.

question: When driving in a work zone, what should you do about following distance?
options: a:Follow the vehicle ahead more closely to keep traffic moving.,b:Avoid tailgating and increase your following distance.,c:Maintain the exact same distance as on open roads.,d:Pass other vehicles as soon as you can.
note: In work zones, traffic may stop or slow suddenly due to workers, equipment, or lane shifts. You should increase your following distance so you have more time and space to react and stop smoothly, reducing the risk of rear-end collisions.

question: Regulatory traffic signs are generally which color background?
options: a:White.,b:Yellow.,c:Green.,d:Blue.
note: Most regulatory signs that state traffic laws, such as speed limit, no parking, or lane use control, have a white background with black or red symbols or letters. However, some regulatory signs use other colors, like red (STOP, YIELD, DO NOT ENTER) or black/white for one-way. The key idea is that white-background signs commonly indicate regulations you must obey.

question: Which message appears on a red, octagonal sign?
options: a:Do not enter.,b:Stop.,c:One-way.
note: A red, octagonal (eight-sided) sign is always a STOP sign. When you see this shape and color, you must come to a complete stop at the stop line, crosswalk, or before entering the intersection, and proceed only when it is safe.

question: When should you not use your horn?
options: a:If you might hit another vehicle.,b:When visibility ahead is limited.,c:Near blind pedestrians.
note: You should avoid using your horn near blind pedestrians because they rely heavily on sound to understand traffic movement. A sudden horn blast can be confusing or startling. Instead, slow down, be prepared to stop, and give them the right-of-way.

question: When properly adjusted, what should your inside rearview mirror show?
options: a:Your own reflection.,b:Only the backseat passengers.,c:The entire rear window.,d:The front of your vehicle.
note: The inside rearview mirror should be adjusted so you can see the entire rear window by moving only your eyes, not your head. This gives you the widest possible view of traffic behind you and helps you check quickly and safely.

question: When should you allow extra following distance behind another vehicle?
options: a:When following a small passenger car.,b:When following a station wagon only.,c:When following a vehicle that cannot see behind it
note: You should leave extra following distance when you are behind vehicles that have limited rear visibility, such as large trucks, buses, RVs, or vehicles towing trailers. These drivers may not see you in their mirrors, and you will also need more space to see around them and to stop safely if they brake suddenly.

section-name: Traffic Laws & Rules of the Road
question: In traffic moving 50–55 mph, when are you least likely to have an accident?
options: a:When you drive several mph faster than most vehicles.,b:When you drive several mph slower than most vehicles.,c:When you travel within that same speed range as other vehicles.
note: In steady traffic, you are generally safest when traveling at about the same speed as surrounding vehicles, as long as you stay within the posted speed limit and adjust for conditions. Large speed differences—either faster or slower—force more lane changes and passing, which increases the risk of collisions.

question: What does a green arrow signal require of drivers?
options: a:Yield to any pedestrians and vehicles already in the intersection.,b:Wait a set number of seconds before moving.,c:Proceed in the arrow's direction after yielding to any vehicles and pedestrians.
